options.denominator: None; raw counts of crash records
options.grouping: Night 18:00–05:59 vs day 06:00–17:59; complete calendar years 2013–2025
options.reason: A newsroom may need the absolute number of reported collisions in equal-length clock windows to describe when crash burden occurs.
options.answer: Among complete years 2013–2025, police reports logged 763,838 crashes at night versus 1,368,380 by day, so recorded crashes were more numerous by day; these counts do not establish per-trip danger.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether more reported crashes occur during nighttime than daytime hours: it counts crashes in equal 12-hour clock windows and shows 763,838 at night versus 1,368,380 by day. A count comparison is a defensible measure of observed crash burden across those equal-length windows, but it does not establish higher per-traveler risk. It leaves unanswered whether a crash is more likely to injure or kill someone, and whether exposure to traffic differs by time. It excludes all 2012 and 2026 records (136,969 rows, 6.04% of the file) to compare complete calendar years 2013–2025; no rows are excluded for missing crash time.

options.metric: Share of crashes involving at least one injured or killed person
options.denominator: Crashes with non-NULL values for both number_of_persons_injured and number_of_persons_killed
options.grouping: Night 18:00–05:59 vs day 06:00–17:59; complete calendar years 2013–2025
options.reason: A newsroom may prefer the share of crashes with reported harm, which compares collision severity without treating every crash as equally consequential.
options.answer: 28.05% of nighttime crashes involved an injury or death versus 22.77% of daytime crashes (1.23 times the daytime share), although this is severity conditional on a reported crash rather than per-trip risk.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether a reported crash was more likely to involve injury or death at night: the share is 28.05% at night and 22.77% by day. This binary crash-level outcome is a defensible, easily interpreted measure of reported harm conditional on a crash. It leaves unanswered the risk per trip or mile, because the file contains no traffic-exposure denominator. It excludes all 2012 and 2026 records (136,969 rows, 6.04% of the file) for complete-year comparison, plus 29 daytime rows (0.0021%) and 13 nighttime rows (0.0017%) in 2013–2025 because at least one required injury/death field is NULL.

options.metric: Share of crashes with at least one person killed
options.grouping: Night 18:00–05:59 vs day 06:00–17:59; complete calendar years 2013–2025
options.reason: A separate fatal-crash share isolates the most consequential outcome and shows whether nighttime collisions are disproportionately fatal.
options.answer: Fatal crashes made up 0.245% of nighttime crashes (1,869/763,826) versus 0.102% by day (1,402/1,368,356), about 2.39 times the daytime share; this is not per-trip risk.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether a reported crash was more likely to be fatal at night: fatal crashes were 0.245% of nighttime crashes and 0.102% of daytime crashes. Fatality share is a defensible severity indicator focused on the most consequential crash outcome. It leaves unanswered the chance of being killed per trip or mile, since the file has no traffic-exposure denominator. It excludes all 2012 and 2026 records (136,969 rows, 6.04% of the file) for complete-year comparison, plus 24 daytime rows (0.0018%) and 12 nighttime rows (0.0016%) in 2013–2025 because number_of_persons_killed is NULL.
